catalog_quote: The default stress pattern in Osage has primary stress on the peninitial syllable, followed by secondary stress on every other syllable [p. 5] ... there are words with initial stress in Osage (see (5)); primary stress never surfaces on a syllable other than the first two (i.e. the 'window' for primary stress is the first two syllables). [p. 6] ... As illustrated in (22), two stress patterns were observed: (i) the first syllable is stressed and every other odd-numbered syllable carries secondary stress, and (ii) the second syllable is stressed and every other even-numbered syllable carries secondary stress. In sum, stress always alternates; there is neither clash nor lapse [p. 13] ... Note that stress rather than tone is lexically specified because there is no tonal contrast in the language ... tone is completely predictable from stress [p. 21] ... (35a) and (35b) are minimal pairs differing solely in the placement of stress on the surface. [p. 23] ... I conclude that the default pattern in Osage cannot be initial stress. Instead, the default is peninitial stress; all forms with initial stress on the surface are lexically marked. [p. 25] ... Here we see LHL and HLL sequences respectively, but stress differs in its location, showing that a weight distinction among the syllables is not a factor in placement of stress. [p. 26]

new_statements.quote: The default stress pattern in Osage has primary stress on the peninitial syllable, followed by secondary stress on every other syllable [...] An alternative hypothesis is to say that the default pattern is initial stress and that peninitial stress is lexically marked. At first glance, there seems to be some support for this view since there are words with initial stress in Osage (see (5)); primary stress never surfaces on a syllable other than the first two (i.e. the 'window' for primary stress is the first two syllables). [p. 13:] As illustrated in (22), two stress patterns were observed: (i) the first syllable is stressed and every other odd-numbered syllable carries secondary stress, and (ii) the second syllable is stressed and every other even-numbered syllable carries secondary stress. In sum, stress always alternates; there is neither clash nor lapse

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls by default on the second syllable of the word, with secondary stresses on every second syllable after it (left-to-right iambs, insensitive to vowel length); a lexically marked minority of words/morpheme combinations carry primary stress on the first syllable instead (then secondaries on odd syllables). Primary stress is confined to a two-syllable window at the left edge. High tone accompanies stressed syllables and unstressed initial syllables and is fully predictable from stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rhythmic: on every other syllable following the primary (4th, 6th.. in default words; 3rd, 5th.. in initial-stress words); author assumes no lexical secondary stress (fn. 9); based on words of up to five syllables (fn. 7).
new_statements.exceptions: Words with surface initial stress (e.g. 'count them!', 'he's sick with', 'horseback riding', 'to yell', 'moon', ex. (5)) are analysed as carrying lexical stress on the first syllable; affixal alternations (P3P wa- vs valence wa-, A2S infix) are used to argue that the second syllable, not the first, is the default position (sections 3.1-3.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation/recorded forms (isolated words, greetings, prayer, vocabulary lists recorded by Quintero 1977-2001, speakers from Osage County OK); acoustic correlates measured (duration, amplitude, F0). Wolff 1952 (IJAL 18:65), the older primary source, instead treated stress as an unpredictable phoneme without stating a position.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Osage proper (osag1243), the Dhegiha Siouan language of Osage County, Oklahoma; Altshuler's data are Quintero's 1977-2001 recordings of the last L1 speakers (no dialect split relevant to stress; Wolff 1952 distinguishes two idiolect groups (L)/(B) only for juncture phonetics). No separate glottocode issue.

sources.locator: p. 5 (section 1, Introduction); also p. 13 (section 2.4) and pp. 21-25 (section 3)
sources.note: Default primary stress on the peninitial (second) syllable with secondary stress on every other syllable thereafter; a lexically marked class of words has initial stress (then odd-numbered secondaries); primary stress never falls outside the first two syllables; stress always alternates (no clash/lapse); tone (H on stressed and on unstressed initial syllables) is predictable from stress; vowel length does not affect stress (quantity-insensitive iambs). Supported by duration/amplitude/F0 measurements from Quintero's recordings (pp. 5, 13, 21-25).

sources.note: Treats stress as phonemic: 'Stressed and unstressed syllables alternate at irregular intervals throughout any Osage utterance. We therefore distinguish a phoneme of primary stress /'/.. Single morpheme utterances have no more than one stressed syllable. A secondary stress, phonemically distinct from /'/, may occur, but the limited text material did not permit definite identification'. No placement rule given.
